title: The beasts (Revelation 13)
hookLine: empire as a beast demanding worship; many read 666 as a code for Nero

lines: A BEAST RISES FROM THE SEA.
WHO IS LIKE UNTO THE BEAST?
cards: Six hundred threescore and six. That number has set off a great deal of guessing, and it comes from one verse at the end of Revelation thirteen. But before the number, there's a crowd.

A beast has risen out of the sea, and the whole world follows it in wonder. People bow down, chanting the kind of question you shout at a rally: "Who is like unto the beast? who is able to make war with him?"
Today's word is that beast, and the one that comes after it.

teach.h: A SONG FOR GOD, SUNG TO A BEAST.
teach.b: First, the chant is borrowed. After the sea crossing in Exodus, Moses and Israel sang: "Who is like unto thee, O LORD, among the gods?" The crowd takes a song meant for God and sings it to a beast.
That's the beast's whole project: to be worshiped. It's given power, the text says, over every kindred and tongue and nation.

teach.h: HORNS LIKE A LAMB, VOICE OF A DRAGON.
teach.b: Second, another beast comes up out of the earth: "he had two horns like a lamb, and he spake as a dragon." It looks gentle and sounds like something else.
Its job is to make everyone worship the first beast, and to see that no one can buy or sell without its mark.
Third, the number: "Let him that hath understanding count the number of the beast: for it is the number of a man." Some readers hear a code for Nero, the Roman emperor.
Others read a symbol: a number that keeps falling short. Others again wait for a figure still to come. The text itself only says it is the number of a man.
Fourth, what John says to do.
Not panic, not decode: "Here is the patience and the faith of the saints." Some readers carry the chapter into ordinary life: the beast need not look like a monster.
It can be any power that asks for more than loyalty, that wants worship. And it can look like a lamb.

how: Christians read Revelation 13 in different ways: some as a word about Rome in John's own day, some as a pattern that repeats whenever power asks to be worshiped, and some as a picture of events still to come.

games.q: the whole world follows the beast, chanting, who is able to make war with him? you're one of John's readers. what does the chapter tell you to do?
o: fight back with the beast's own weapons.
hold on with patience and faith.
work out the number before anything else.
games.why: "here is the patience and the faith of the saints." the chapter asks for endurance, not panic and not codebreaking.

practice: Think back over the week to where something asked more of you than it should: a job that wants your whole evening, a screen that wants you every few minutes, a leader, a party or a crowd that asks you never to question it.

Don't judge yourself; just see it plainly, the way John saw a lamb's horns and heard a dragon's voice. If you pray, name it to God and give your loyalty back where you believe it belongs; if not, name it to yourself.

wordCard.voice: The beasts. In Revelation thirteen, one from the sea that wants worship, and one from the earth that looks like a lamb and speaks like a dragon.

orig.note: Greek: a wild beast, the word for both creatures in Revelation 13.

carryVoice: Your line: don't bow to the beast. Patience and faith, not panic. Rest well.
